d.title: It printed “starting”, then failed on a name nothing had checked
d.caption: **A compiled language like Java or Rust would have refused to build this file at all. Python ran most of it happily and failed at the exact moment it needed a name that did not exist** — and that is not sloppiness, it is a direct consequence of how Python turns text into behaviour. **The typo `totl` is grammatically fine — a perfectly legal name — so compilation had no objection.** Only the `return` instruction looked it up, **and it reached that instruction on the empty list too, because a `for` loop over nothing still falls through to what follows.**

The name is looked up at RUNTIME
And the empty list reaches it too

d.title: A document on one side, a program on the other
d.caption: **“Python” names two different things, and conflating them causes real confusion later.** The split matters because **the implementations differ in exactly the places engineers care about: speed, memory, concurrency and C-library compatibility.** Two specifics worth holding onto: **the language does not mandate a Global Interpreter Lock — CPython has one — and the language does not mandate reference counting — CPython uses it.** So “Python has a GIL” is a statement about a program, not about a language.

d.title: Three famous behaviours, each derivable from the pipeline
d.caption: **All three are usually presented as trivia and all three follow from one model.** The first is narrowing but not closing: **since 3.11 the interpreter is adaptive — it notices a `BINARY_OP` keeps seeing two ints and rewrites that instruction in place to an int-only version, skipping the type dispatch — which is a real speedup and still not C.** The third has the sharpest practical edge: **the lock is released around I/O, so while a thread waits on a socket, a file or a database another thread runs — which is precisely why threads help enormously for network-bound work and not at all for computation.**

items.label: Why Python is slower than C in tight numeric loops
items.desc: BINARY_OP must inspect both types, find the right add, call it, allocate a result and manage refcounts.

items.label: Why a typo in a rare branch reaches production
items.desc: The compiler validated your grammar, not your names — nothing checks the name exists until it runs.

items.label: Why threads do not speed up pure-Python compute
items.desc: Only one thread may execute bytecode at any instant, so two numeric loops take turns.

d.title: Two of these four are guaranteed and two are not
d.caption: **Bytecode is an implementation detail with no stability guarantee — opcodes are added, removed and renamed between minor versions, 3.11 rewrote large parts of the interpreter, and 3.12 and 3.13 changed opcodes again.** So the line to hold is between **what `for` and `+` mean, which is stable across versions *and* implementations**, and **the specific opcode names, which are never safe in shipped code.** The `.pyc` format makes the point for you: **it is versioned in the filename for exactly this reason.**

d.title: One line of output is the authoritative answer; the rest is inference
d.caption: **A typical machine has several Python installations that know nothing about each other, and typing `python` picks whichever appears first on your `PATH`** — so the habit worth building on day one is: never assume, ask. **`sys.executable` is the authoritative answer; everything else is inference.** Two details that save hours: **`sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix` is the reliable venv test**, and **`sys.version_info` is a comparable tuple — use it rather than string comparison, because `"3.9" > "3.10"` is `True` as strings and wrong as versions.**

d.title: The system Python runs the system
d.caption: **Linux distributions and macOS ship a Python that the operating system itself depends on — package managers, system utilities and parts of the desktop are written in it.** So the rule is simple and absolute: **the system Python runs the system; you install your own and you work inside virtual environments.** The failure mode is worth picturing: **`sudo pip install` into the system interpreter can upgrade a package a system tool depended on, and the thing that breaks is not your project.**

nodes.label: The OS depends on its Python
sudo pip install upgrades a shared package

d.title: The question is not whether a package exists
d.caption: **Python's “batteries included” is earned — JSON, CSV, HTTP, SQLite, compression, hashing, dates, subprocesses, threading, async, testing and argument parsing are all in the standard library, and a large amount of professional Python needs nothing else.** PyPI adds several hundred thousand packages, **so the engineering question is not *does a package exist* — one always does — but *should this be a dependency*.** The two ends of the list are the clearest: **`zoneinfo` retired most date libraries, and there is no standard-library answer at all for array maths.**

d.title: VS Code does not read your shell's PATH
d.caption: **It has its own notion of the selected interpreter, and every Python feature — IntelliSense, the linter, the debugger, the test runner — follows that setting rather than your terminal.** Which produces the characteristic symptom: **red squiggles under imports that work perfectly when you run the file.** Fix it once per project by committing the setting, so every contributor gets the same behaviour. And **`typeCheckingMode: basic` turns on real checking without the noise of `strict` on an untyped codebase** — it catches undefined names as you type, which is 1.1's deferred-name problem caught early.

nodes.label: The editor uses its own setting

d.title: A kernel list belongs to your user account, not to the project
d.caption: **Jupyter has its own indirection: a kernel is a registered interpreter, and the registry is global to your user account rather than scoped to a directory.** So **a notebook can quietly run against an interpreter that has nothing to do with the project directory it lives in** — which is exactly why **a notebook works for you and fails for a colleague who cloned the same repository.** The fix is to register the project's venv as a named kernel and select it deliberately, so the notebook records which interpreter it expects.

d.title: Five things to settle in the REPL rather than guess at
d.caption: **The interactive interpreter is where small questions belong — what does this method return, what shape is this data, does this regex match — and reaching for it is faster than writing a script and far faster than guessing.** The row most people have not met is the fourth: **`python -i script.py` runs the script and then leaves you in a REPL with all its variables still alive**, which is the cheapest way there is to inspect state after a failure. And **IPython costs one install and pays from the first session.**

d.title: Same id, same type, new value — then a different id entirely
d.caption: **Identity and type are fixed for an object's whole life; only value can change, and only for mutable types.** The first two rows are one object mutated — **id `…91200` both times** — and the third is a different object at `…94016`. Which is the distinction the whole lesson rests on: **`x = 5` followed by `x = "five"` does not change an object, it binds `x` to a different one.** `is` compares the first column; `==` compares the third.

d.title: The second call returns ['apple', 'banana'], and most people expect ['banana']
d.caption: **Default arguments are evaluated once, when the `def` statement executes — not on each call** — which comes straight from 1.1: the `def` is an instruction that runs, and it builds the default at that moment. **So that empty list is created a single time and stored on the function object, and every call that omits the argument binds to *that same list*.** The last row is proof rather than explanation: **`func.__defaults__` is `(['apple', 'banana'],)`, so the accumulated state is printable.**

d.title: `tags or DEFAULT_TAGS` does not copy the default
d.caption: This is the shape the bug takes in a real codebase, **where the two names are far apart.** The expression **binds the new document's `tags` key to the module-level list — so every document created without tags shares one list, and the module constant is corrupted for the lifetime of the process.** The output shows it: **two documents, and appending to one changes both.** The fix is §04's fix: **`list(DEFAULT_TAGS)`, or `None` as the sentinel and build the list inside.**

nodes.label: And the module constant is corrupted
Fix: list(DEFAULT_TAGS), or a None sentinel

d.title: Four operators where the answer is not what C taught you
d.caption: **An `int` grows to whatever size memory allows — `100!` is 302 digits and exact, where most languages would have wrapped silently.** The operators carry their own surprises, and two are worth internalising: **`//` rounds toward negative infinity, so `-7 // 2` is `-4` and not `-3`; and `%` carries the sign of the *divisor*, so `-7 % 3` is `2` in Python and `-1` in C and Java.** Which means **a bucket index computed with `%` behaves differently in a Python reimplementation of a C algorithm.**

d.title: Four falsy values that mean four different things
d.caption: **`None` is a singleton — there is exactly one instance in the process, which is why `is None` is the correct test — and its job is to represent the absence of a value, which is a different statement from zero or empty.** The user example makes it operational: **a user who has never logged in has `last_login = None`; a user with no items has `item_count = 0`; a user who cleared their bio has `bio = ""`.** All four are falsy, **so `if not x` collapses all four into one branch** — which is the bug this section exists to prevent.

d.title: Five specs, and the last two replace most debug printing
d.caption: The alignment and separator specs are what make log output readable, **and `{x=}` is the one worth adopting immediately: `f"{score=}"` prints `score=0.87241`, which replaces almost every `print("score:", score)` you would otherwise write** — including over an expression, as `len(items)=2`. And **`!r` uses `repr()` rather than `str()`, which is what you want in logs and errors, because the quoting is what distinguishes `""` from `" "`.**

state: an expression, not just a name

d.title: Eleven tiers, and one of them is where the bugs are
d.caption: **You do not need to memorise the table — you need the handful of places where the answer is not obvious, and to parenthesise there.** The surprise is tier 6: **the bitwise operators are looser than arithmetic and tighter than comparison, so `a & b == c` parses as `a & (b == c)`**, which is almost never what was meant. Two more worth knowing: **`**` is right-associative, so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is 512 rather than 64**, and **unary minus binds looser than `**`, so `-2 ** 2` is `-4`.**

d.title: Three conversions that lose data without raising
d.caption: The rows that raise are the easy ones — **`int("3.5")` is a `ValueError`, loudly.** The dangerous rows are silent: **`int(3.9)` is `3` because it truncates toward zero rather than rounding; `bool("False")` is `True` because it only tests emptiness; and `str(x)` never fails, which is why a bug can travel a long way as the string `"None"`.** And **`dict` from pairs lets a later duplicate key overwrite an earlier one silently**, which is how a config merge loses an entry.

d.title: The annotated function ran and returned 15
d.caption: **Type hints let you write down what a function expects, and Python ignores them during execution — `repeat(5, 3)` on a function annotated `(str, int) -> str` runs and returns `15`.** So what they do is real and entirely static: **document the contract, drive editor autocomplete and refactoring, and let a checker such as mypy find mismatches without running the code.** What closes the gap is two tools for two different problems: **mypy in CI for your own code, and Pydantic at the boundary where data arrives from outside and runtime validation genuinely is required.**

d.title: Four keyword arguments, and one of them is a production concern
d.caption: `sep`, `end` and `file` are conveniences — **`sep=''` gives `abc`, `sep='-'` builds `2024-01-15` from parts, and `end=''` suppresses the newline.** **`flush=True` is the one that matters outside a terminal: stdout is line-buffered to a console and block-buffered to a pipe or a file, so a crash can lose everything printed since the last flush** — which is why a log line that definitely executed is missing from captured output. In production the answer is not `flush`, **it is `logging`.**

d.title: input() always returns a string, and strips only the newline
d.caption: **`input()` returns `"30"` and never an `int`**, so every numeric input needs parsing — with exactly the errors 1.8 measured. And the detail that bites: **it strips the trailing newline and nothing else, so leading and trailing spaces survive**, which is why `.strip()` before parsing is routine rather than defensive. The error path is worth copying as written: **report to `stderr` with `!r` so the offending value is quoted, then `raise SystemExit(1)`** — a message on stdout with a zero exit code is a failure the caller cannot detect.

nodes.label: And raise SystemExit(1)
nodes.sub: or the caller cannot detect it

d.title: Eight commands, and two of them are why a debugger beats a print
d.caption: **Adding a print, re-running, discovering you needed a different variable, and repeating is a slow loop — `breakpoint()` stops execution and gives you a REPL with every local in scope**, so the next question costs one line instead of one run. The two rows no amount of printing replaces are the last: **`u` and `d` move up and down the stack to inspect a *caller's* locals**, which is where the wrong value usually came from.
